title: When Steadiness Carries You: Resonance, Rhythm and Coherence
reflection: This week choose one resonance, steady one rhythm and bring your parts into step: protect one rhythm daily, check that your words, feeling and intention point the same way, and notice who and what tunes you up or down.

questions.q: What is resonance, in the picture of pushing a child on a swing?
o: A hard shove, given as strongly as you can, so that the swing is carried high by sheer force.
Matching your rhythm to the thing’s own, so that a tiny push at the right moment gives a huge effect.
Letting the swing come to rest, so that nothing you do can ever work against its own motion.
Pushing at random moments, so that no pattern builds up that the swing could settle into.
questions.e: Shove hard at random and you fight the swing; a small push in time with each arc makes it grow on almost no effort. The same law runs a radio tuned to its station, and makes soldiers break step on certain bridges. Match the frequency, and energy flows.
questions.c: Resonance: matched rhythm, small input, large effect

questions.q: Kai asks whether his mood is partly just whoever he has been standing next to. What does Swamiji say?
o: More than most people realise: you cannot switch resonance off, so it is worth choosing what you stand near.
No: mood comes wholly from within, and other people have no real part in what a person feels.
Yes, and so the only safe course is to keep away from other people as much as can be done.
Only a little, and only in children, since grown people have their own settled rhythms of mood.
questions.e: You are always resonating with something: beside a calm person you settle, beside a fearful one you are pulled. The protection is to become a fine tuning fork, not a loose string that buzzes at every sound. That is not coldness; it is selectivity earned through practice.
questions.c: You cannot switch resonance off; choose it

questions.q: “You can stop resonating with the people around you by deciding not to be affected by them.”
questions.e: You cannot switch resonance off. You can only choose what you place yourself near, and train the mind to be tuned and selective, powerfully responsive to what is true and unmoved by what is trivial or false.

questions.q: Kai has slept badly for weeks and asks whether he should simply sleep more. How does Swamiji answer?
o: Sleep is a real part of it, and rhythm itself is a stable floor, which aligning with pays back fast.
Sleep does not matter, since the mind is able to make up for any loss of rest by thinking harder.
Only sleep matters, and nothing else in the day, such as meals or breath, can have any effect.
He must wait until his mood lifts, because nothing in daily routine could change how he feels.
questions.e: Fighting your rhythms, with erratic sleep, meals at odd hours and nights turned to days, has a real cost. Slowing the breath to about six a minute shifts the body toward calm within minutes. A steady rhythm is the floor everything finer stands on.
questions.c: Rhythm is the floor that calm rides on

questions.q: A person is stimulated, racing and never settling, with no steady pulse. Which of the three rhythms is this?
o: Sattva, since a person who is busy and active is the clearest case of a steady, harmonious beat.
Rajas: a fast, erratic over-activity that is stimulated but never settles, with no steady pulse.
Tamas, since racing about without settling is only another form of a heavy and sluggish beat.
None of the three, since the guṇas describe a person’s character and not a passing state.
questions.e: Sattva is a steady, harmonious beat where thought, feeling and action keep time. Rajas is fast and erratic. Tamas is a collapsed, heavy slowness that looks like rest but is stuckness. Steady practices restore a healthy beat first.
questions.c: The guṇas are three kinds of rhythm

questions.q: “Regular sleep, regular meals and a slow breath are plain, but rhythm itself is a powerful medicine.”
questions.e: Dr Watson need not be embarrassed. A system in steady rhythm is stable and resilient, so small knocks do not capsize it; one with no reliable rhythm is fragile. Before any subtle work, giving a struggling person back their rhythm has already done a great deal.

questions.q: What does the bulb and laser picture show about coherence?
o: The laser uses far more energy than the bulb, so it needs a stronger source to give its beam.
The same energy has a very different power when the waves are lined up in step, as in a laser.
The bulb is the better light for living in, since a laser is too hard and narrow to be of use.
A laser works only on steel, so the picture has nothing to say about thought or feeling.
questions.e: They can pour out the same energy. The bulb scatters its light in all directions, a soft glow; the laser lines every wave up, and the same energy cuts steel. When thought, feeling and action line up, the inner fighting stops and energy stops leaking.
questions.c: Same energy, different power when in step

questions.q: Sarah is often thinking one thing, feeling another and doing a third, and is exhausted. What is the practice?
o: Check coherence before a hard talk: do my words, my feeling and my intention point the same way?
Push her feelings aside so that thought alone leads, since feelings are what divide a person.
Do as many things as she can at once, so that no single thread is left to pull the others apart.
Say nothing in hard talks, since she cannot be sure of any of the three being in line.
questions.e: The absence of coherence is why it drains her: she is a bulb. When the parts line up she feels strangely powerful at a hard task. And the coherent mind sees more truly, because it is no longer at war with itself enough to distort the view.
questions.c: Check that thought, feeling and intention are in line

questions.q: Swamiji says a group field can be powerful. What caution goes with it?
o: It amplifies whatever is put into it, so a gathering of truth lifts everyone and one of rage can carry them off.
It is always good, since people who act together will find that they act well, whatever their aim.
It is always harmful, since a person’s own judgment is lost as soon as he joins any group.
It has no real effect, since people in a room are no more than separate minds that sit near.
questions.e: The Ṛgveda hymn is a recipe for people moving, speaking and intending together. The power is real and neutral. That is why discernment must walk alongside: what matters is what you let it amplify.
questions.c: A group field amplifies what is put into it

questions.q: James is asked to steady his own breath and presence at one tense moment in class. What does he watch for?
o: Whether the room entrains toward him, rather than he toward the tension in it.
Whether the pupils notice that he is breathing slowly and ask him to explain what he is doing.
Whether the tension passes in time, whatever he may have done with his own breath.
Whether he can force the class to be quiet by the sheer calm of his manner.
questions.e: A steady wave tends to bring the rhythms near it into step, as with pendulums on a shelf. James is the steadiest wave in his classroom whether he means to be or not; this week he does it on purpose.
questions.c: Be the steady wave on purpose
